claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,D.

claims.claim: Wnt5a treatment results in a reduction of mAPP in the TGN after 2 hr and 4 hr.
claims.source: However, we found a reduction of mAPP in the TGN, accompanied by an increase of mAPP in lysosomes both after 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G) and 4 hr (Figure 3B,D,E) of Wnt5a treatment suggesting that Wnt5a regulates intracellular targeting of mAPP after internalization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figures 3B,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G.

claims.claim: Wnt5a treatment results in an increase of mAPP in lysosomes after 2 hr and 4 hr.
claims.source: However, we found a reduction of mAPP in the TGN, accompanied by an increase of mAPP in lysosomes both after 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G) and 4 hr (Figure 3B,D,E) of Wnt5a treatment suggesting that Wnt5a regulates intracellular targeting of mAPP after internalization.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figures 3B,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: Wnt5a regulates intracellular targeting of mAPP after internalization.
claims.source: However, we found a reduction of mAPP in the TGN, accompanied by an increase of mAPP in lysosomes both after 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G) and 4 hr (Figure 3B,D,E) of Wnt5a treatment suggesting that Wnt5a regulates intracellular targeting of mAPP after internalization.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the changes in mAPP localization to TGN and lysosomes upon Wnt5a treatment.

claims.claim: The expression levels of Rab5, Golgin97, and Lamp1 are not affected by Wnt5a treatment.
claims.source: Importantly, the levels of expression of these markers (Rab5, Golgin97, and Lamp1) are not affected by Wnt5a treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The level of fl-mAPP is significantly reduced after 4 hr of Wnt5a treatment.
claims.source: We found that the level of fl-mAPP was significantly reduced after 4 hr of Wnt5a treatment, as shown by western blot (Figure 3F,G), with no effect on mApp mRNA levels (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 3F,G.

claims.claim: Wnt5a treatment has no effect on mApp mRNA levels.
claims.source: We found that the level of fl-mAPP was significantly reduced after 4 hr of Wnt5a treatment, as shown by western blot (Figure 3F,G), with no effect on mApp mRNA levels (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: The decrease of mAPP upon Wnt5a treatment is caused by lysosomal degradation.
claims.source: The results of immunofluorescence (IF) and western blot (WB) suggest that the decrease of the mAPP upon Wnt5a treatment is caused by lysosomal degradation.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined immunofluorescence and western blot data showing increased lysosomal localization and decreased total mAPP levels.

claims.claim: Bafilomycin-A treatment restores mAPP to control levels after Wnt5a treatment.
claims.source: To confirm this, we used Bafilomycin-A in combination with Wnt5a treatment. Bafilomycin-A treatment was performed 1 hr after Wnt5a addition as Wnt5a treatment already affected APP levels after 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 5)- to inhibit the lysosome and found that this restored mAPP to control levels (Figure 3I–L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 3I-L.

claims.claim: Non-canonical Wnt5a-PCP signaling reduces mAPP stability.
claims.source: These data suggest that non-canonical Wnt5a-PCP signaling reduces mAPP stability.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing Wnt5a-induced reduction in mAPP levels that is rescued by lysosomal inhibition.

claims.claim: fl-mAPP and Wnt3a co-immunoprecipitate in a CRD-dependent fashion.
claims.source: To test this, we performed IP experiments with Wnt3a. We found that fl-mAPP and Wnt3a co-IP in a CRD-dependent fashion (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The fraction of mAPP co-localized with early endosomes is not affected after 2 hr and 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.source: As shown in and Figure 3—figure supplement 2(A), The fraction of mAPP co-localized with early endosomes (Figure 4B,C) and recycling endosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,D) was not affected after 2 hr and 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figures 4B,C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Wnt3a treatment has no effect on mAPP co-localization with recycling endosomes after 2 hr and 4 hr.
claims.source: As shown in and Figure 3—figure supplement 2(A), The fraction of mAPP co-localized with early endosomes (Figure 4B,C) and recycling endosome (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,D) was not affected after 2 hr and 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,D.

claims.claim: More mAPP is present in the TGN after 2 hr and 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.source: However, more mAPP was present in the TGN, with no effect on the lysosomal mAPP fraction after 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G) and 4 hr (Figure 4B–E) of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figures 4B,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: Wnt3a treatment has no effect on the lysosomal mAPP fraction after 2 hr and 4 hr.
claims.source: However, more mAPP was present in the TGN, with no effect on the lysosomal mAPP fraction after 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D,G) and 4 hr (Figure 4B–E) of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figures 4B,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claims.claim: The expression levels of Rab5, Golgin97, and Lamp1 are not affected after Wnt3a treatment.
claims.source: The expression levels of Rab5, Golgin97 and Lamp1 were not affected after Wnt3a treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Western blot analysis shows increased fl-mAPP upon Wnt3a treatment.
claims.source: Western blot analysis showed increased fl-mAPP upon Wnt3a treatment (Figure 4F,G), but no effect on mRNA levels (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4F,G.

claims.claim: Wnt3a treatment has no effect on mApp mRNA levels.
claims.source: Western blot analysis showed increased fl-mAPP upon Wnt3a treatment (Figure 4F,G), but no effect on mRNA levels (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Retromer inhibitor (LY294002) reverses the effect of Wnt3a on mAPP trafficking and protein levels.
claims.source: To test whether Wnt3a regulates mAPP retro trafficking to the TGN, we co-treated primary neurons with Wnt3a and a retromer inhibitor (LY294002), retromer inhibitor treatment was performed 1 hr after Wnt3a addition as Wnt3a treatment could affected APP protein expression clearly 2 hr later (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). This reversed the effect of Wnt3a on mAPP trafficking protein levels (Figure 4I–L).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4I-L.

claims.claim: Simultaneous treatment with Wnt3a and Wnt5a results in no change to APP protein levels compared to controls.
claims.source: Then, we tested the effects of simultaneous treatment with Wnt3a and Wnt5a. This resulted in no change to APP protein levels compared to controls, suggesting that Wnt3a and Wnt5a neutralize each other's effects on mAPP (Figure 4M,N), again with no effects on mRNA levels (Figure 4O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 4M,N.

claims.claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a neutralize each other's effects on mAPP.
claims.source: Then, we tested the effects of simultaneous treatment with Wnt3a and Wnt5a. This resulted in no change to APP protein levels compared to controls, suggesting that Wnt3a and Wnt5a neutralize each other's effects on mAPP (Figure 4M,N), again with no effects on mRNA levels (Figure 4O).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of change in APP levels when both Wnts are applied together.

claims.claim: Simultaneous treatment with Wnt3a and Wnt5a has no effects on mApp mRNA levels.
claims.source: Then, we tested the effects of simultaneous treatment with Wnt3a and Wnt5a. This resulted in no change to APP protein levels compared to controls, suggesting that Wnt3a and Wnt5a neutralize each other's effects on mAPP (Figure 4M,N), again with no effects on mRNA levels (Figure 4O).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4O.

claims.claim: APP is a key component in both Wnt canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling.
claims.source: We and others have previously shown that APP is a key component in both Wnt canonical and non-canonical Wnt signaling (Elliott et al., 2018; Soldano et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors and others.

claims.claim: Treatment with Wnt3a results in β-catenin accumulation in APP-WT, but not APP-KO, primary cortical neurons at DIV7.
claims.source: We confirmed this in our system and found that treatment with Wnt3a resulted in β-catenin accumulation in APP-WT, but not APP-KO, primary cortical neurons at DIV7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claims.claim: A 4 hr Wnt3a treatment significantly decreases Aβ40/42 production.
claims.source: Our data show that a 4 hr Wnt3a/5a treatment has a long-lasting effect on Aβ40/42 production and that those effects are antagonistic. Consistent with Wnt3a favoring recycling of APP, we found that Wnt3a treatment significantly decrease Aβ40/42 production (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Aβ detection data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claims.claim: Wnt5a treatment results in an increase in Aβ40/42 production.
claims.source: In contrast, Wnt5a treatment, which induces APP internalization into acidic compartments, resulted in an increase in Aβ40/42 production (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Aβ detection data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claims.claim: Wnt3a and Wnt5a have antagonistic effects on Aβ40/42 production.
claims.source: Our data show that a 4 hr Wnt3a/5a treatment has a long-lasting effect on Aβ40/42 production and that those effects are antagonistic.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the opposite effects of Wnt3a and Wnt5a on Aβ production.

claims.claim: Wnt3a also binds to mAPP via the CRD and regulates mAPP trafficking and expression.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that Wnt3a also binds to mAPP via the CRD and regulates mAPP trafficking and expression and that Wnt5a and Wnt3a act antagonistically to regulate APP protein homeostasis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined co-IP, trafficking, and expression data.

claims.claim: Wnt5a and Wnt3a act antagonistically to regulate APP protein homeostasis.
claims.source: Taken together, these data indicate that Wnt3a also binds to mAPP via the CRD and regulates mAPP trafficking and expression and that Wnt5a and Wnt3a act antagonistically to regulate APP protein homeostasis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the opposite effects of Wnt3a and Wnt5a on APP levels and trafficking.

claims.claim: In neurons transduced with wild-type mAPP, mAPP expression can be increased and decreased by Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatments, respectively.
claims.source: In neurons transduced with wild-type mAPP, we confirmed that mAPP expression could be increased and decreased by Wnt3a and Wnt5a treatments, respectively (Figure 5A,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 5A,C.

claims.claim: In neurons transduced with mAPPΔCRD, the effects of Wnt3a and Wnt5a on mAPP expression are eliminated.
claims.source: In contrast, in neurons transduced with mAPPΔCRD those effects were eliminated (Figure 5B,D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figures 5B,D.

claims.claim: Neurons transduced with wild type mAPP show more mAPP in the TGN upon 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment.
claims.source: Neurons transduced with wild type mAPP showed the same results as wild-type neurons with more mAPP in the TGN upon 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment and more mAPP in lysosomes upon 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,E,H) and 4 hr of Wnt5a treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E.

claims.claim: Neurons transduced with wild type mAPP show more mAPP in lysosomes upon 2 hr and 4 hr of Wnt5a treatment.
claims.source: Neurons transduced with wild type mAPP showed the same results as wild-type neurons with more mAPP in the TGN upon 4 hr of Wnt3a treatment and more mAPP in lysosomes upon 2 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B,E,H) and 4 hr of Wnt5a treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claims.claim: All effects of Wnts on mAPP trafficking are abolished in neurons transduced with mAPPΔCRD.
claims.source: All these effects were abolished in neurons transduced with mAPPΔCRD (Figure 5E–H; Figure 3—figure supplement 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,F,I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence colocalization data shown in Figures 5E-H and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The CRD of mAPP is critical for Wnt3a/5a binding and mediates the effects of Wnts on mAPP trafficking and expression.
claims.source: In summary, these data show that the CRD of mAPP is critical for Wnt3a/5a binding and mediates the effects of Wnts on mAPP trafficking and expression.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing loss of Wnt effects when CRD is deleted.

claims.claim: At DIV2, there is no effect of mAPP knockout on initial neurite outgrowth.
claims.source: While we found no effect on initial outgrowth at DIV2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F), at DIV3 mAPP knockout neurons exhibit increased axonal outgrowth compared to controls reflected in three parameters: total axon length, longest axon length, and the number of branch tips (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-F.

claims.claim: At DIV3, mAPP knockout neurons exhibit increased axonal outgrowth compared to controls in total axon length, longest axon length, and number of branch tips.
claims.source: While we found no effect on initial outgrowth at DIV2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–F), at DIV3 mAPP knockout neurons exhibit increased axonal outgrowth compared to controls reflected in three parameters: total axon length, longest axon length, and the number of branch tips (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 6B-E.

claims.claim: At DIV3, dendritic outgrowth in mAPP knockout neurons is not different from controls.
claims.source: In contrast, dendritic outgrowth was not different from controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-C.

claims.claim: Increased axonal length and axonal branch tips in mAPP knockout neurons are rescued by fl-mAPP but not by mAPPΔCRD at DIV3.
claims.source: Increased axonal length and axonal branch tips were rescued by the fl-mAPP but not by the form lacking the CRD at DIV3 (Figure 6B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 6B-E.

claims.claim: Loss of mAPP increases the numbers of both primary and secondary axonal branches at DIV3.
claims.source: Next, we analyzed axonal branching in greater detail and found that loss of mAPP increased the numbers of both primary and secondary axonal branches at DIV3, an increase that was rescued by fl-mAPP but not by mAPPΔCRD (Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 6F,G.

claims.claim: The increase in primary and secondary axonal branches in mAPP knockout neurons is rescued by fl-mAPP but not by mAPPΔCRD at DIV3.
claims.source: Next, we analyzed axonal branching in greater detail and found that loss of mAPP increased the numbers of both primary and secondary axonal branches at DIV3, an increase that was rescued by fl-mAPP but not by mAPPΔCRD (Figure 6F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 6F,G.

claims.claim: At DIV3, the Axon Complexity Index (ACI) shows a tendency to increase in mAPP knockout neurons that is not significant.
claims.source: Finally, we examined the Axon Complexity Index (ACI) (Wong et al., 2017), which measures the ratio of branches of different orders to total branch number, at DIV3. At this early stage, the ACI showed a tendency to increase in mAPP knockout neurons that was not significant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), likely because both primary and secondary branches show a similar level of increase.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: At DIV3, both primary and secondary branches show a similar level of increase in mAPP knockout neurons.
claims.source: Finally, we examined the Axon Complexity Index (ACI) (Wong et al., 2017), which measures the ratio of branches of different orders to total branch number, at DIV3. At this early stage, the ACI showed a tendency to increase in mAPP knockout neurons that was not significant (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), likely because both primary and secondary branches show a similar level of increase.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the non-significant ACI change despite increases in both branch types.

claims.claim: At DIV3, there are no significant alterations in dendritic length or branching in mAPP knockout neurons.
claims.source: In contrast to axonal growth, we found no significant alterations in dendritic length or branching (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–G) consistent with the fact that the spur in dendritic outgrowth is largely initiated at DIV4 (Polleux and Snider, 2010; Barnes and Polleux, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2E-G and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The spur in dendritic outgrowth is largely initiated at DIV4.
claims.source: In contrast to axonal growth, we found no significant alterations in dendritic length or branching (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–G) consistent with the fact that the spur in dendritic outgrowth is largely initiated at DIV4 (Polleux and Snider, 2010; Barnes and Polleux, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: At DIV7, mAPP knockout neurons show an increased Axon Complexity Index (ACI).
claims.source: By this stage, mAPP knockout neurons showed an increased ACI (Figure 7A,B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 7A,B.

claims.claim: At DIV7, total axonal length, longest axon length, and total number of branch tips are not significantly different in mAPP knockout neurons.
claims.source: In contrast, total axonal length, longest axon length, and the total number of branch tips was not significantly different (Figure 7C–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 7C-E.

claims.claim: The increase in axonal complexity in mAPP knockout neurons at DIV7 is due to a significant reduction in primary branches and a significant increase in secondary branches.
claims.source: The increase in axonal complexity in mAPP knockout neurons was due to a significant reduction in the number of primary branches and a significant increase in the number of secondary branches (Figure 7F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 7F,G.

claims.claim: At DIV7, all axonal phenotypes in mAPP knockout neurons are rescued by fl-mAPP but not mAPPΔCRD.
claims.source: Once again, all phenotypes were rescued by fl-mAPP but not mAPPΔCRD.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 7B-G.

claims.claim: At DIV7, there is no difference in total dendrite length or the size of the longest dendrite in mAPP knockout neurons.
claims.source: We observed no difference in total dendrite length or the size of the longest dendrite (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), but observed a significant decrease in the total number of dendritic processes in mAPP knockout neurons compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: At DIV7, there is a significant decrease in the total number of dendritic processes in mAPP knockout neurons compared to controls.
claims.source: We observed no difference in total dendrite length or the size of the longest dendrite (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B), but observed a significant decrease in the total number of dendritic processes in mAPP knockout neurons compared to controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The reduction in dendritic processes at DIV7 is due to fewer main dendritic processes in mAPP knockout neurons with no effect on primary or secondary dendritic branches.
claims.source: This reduction was due to the presence of fewer main dendritic processes in mAPP knockout neurons but no effect was observed on the primary or secondary dendritic branches (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F.

claims.claim: At DIV7, all dendritic phenotypes in mAPP knockout neurons are rescued by fl-mAPP but not mAPPΔCRD.
claims.source: All phenotypes were rescued by fl-mAPP but not mAPPΔCRD.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The role of APP in neuronal maturation requires the CRD domain.
claims.source: Taken together, our results show that the role of APP in neuronal maturation requires the CRD domain.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing that CRD deletion prevents rescue of APP knockout phenotypes.

claims.claim: On DIV3, Wnt3a treatment significantly increases total axon length, the length of longest axon, and axon branch tips in the presence of fl-APP but not APP-Δ-CRD.
claims.source: On DIV3 Wnt3a treatment significantly increased total axon length, the length of longest axon and axon branch tips in the presence of fl-APP but not APP-Δ-CRD (Figure 8A,B,C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figures 8A,B,C.

claims.claim: APP mediates Wnt3a effects on axonal outgrowth.
claims.source: These data suggest that APP mediates Wnt3a effects on axonal outgrowth.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of Wnt3a effects when APP lacks the CRD.

claims.claim: On DIV3, Wnt5a treatment has no effect in the presence of fl-APP but results in increased axonal length when the CRD domain is removed.
claims.source: In contrast to Wnt3a, Wnt5a treatment had no effect in the presence of fl-APP but resulted in increased axonal length when the CRD domain was removed. These data show that APP normally protects axons from the effects of Wnt5a at this developmental stage and that the CRD is required for this (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: APP normally protects axons from the effects of Wnt5a at DIV3 and the CRD is required for this.
claims.source: In contrast to Wnt3a, Wnt5a treatment had no effect in the presence of fl-APP but resulted in increased axonal length when the CRD domain was removed. These data show that APP normally protects axons from the effects of Wnt5a at this developmental stage and that the CRD is required for this (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the appearance of Wnt5a effects only when CRD is deleted.

claims.claim: APP promotes Wnt3a and antagonizes Wnt5a effects on neurons at DIV3 via the CRD domain.
claims.source: Thus, APP promotes Wnt3a and antagonizes Wnt5a effects on neurons at DIV3 via the CRD domain.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing opposite effects of Wnt3a and Wnt5a that depend on the CRD.

claims.claim: On DIV7, a positive Wnt3a effect on axon complexity is observed in the presence of fl-APP but not APP-Δ-CRD.
claims.source: Similarly, on DIV7 we found a positive Wnt3a effect on axon complexity which was observed in the presence of fl-APP but not APP-Δ-CRD (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: On DIV7, Wnt5a has no effect on axon complexity.
claims.source: In contrast Wnt5a had no effect.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Treatment with either Wnt3a or Wnt5a decreases the number of main dendrites in the presence of fl-APP, and the effect is absent or reversed in the presence of APP-Δ-CRD.
claims.source: Finally, we found that treatment with either Wnt3a or Wnt5a decreases the number of the main dendrites in the presence of fl-APP and the effect is absent or even reversed in the presence of APP-Δ-CRD (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: The CRD of APP is required for Wnt3a/5a to regulate neurite outgrowth in cortical primary neurons.
claims.source: Together, these data show that the CRD of APP is required for Wnt3a/5a to regulate neurite outgrowth in cortical primary neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data showing loss of Wnt effects on neurite outgrowth when CRD is deleted.

claims.claim: APP binds both canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands via a conserved CRD.
claims.source: Here, we identify a previously unknown conserved Wnt receptor function for APP proteins. We show that APP binds both canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands via a conserved CRD and that this binding regulates the levels of full-length APP by regulating its intracellular trafficking from early endosomes to the trans Golgi network versus the lysosome.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined co-IP and trafficking data presented in the study.

claims.claim: Wnt binding to APP regulates the levels of full-length APP by regulating its intracellular trafficking from early endosomes to the trans Golgi network versus the lysosome.
claims.source: Here, we identify a previously unknown conserved Wnt receptor function for APP proteins. We show that APP binds both canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands via a conserved CRD and that this binding regulates the levels of full-length APP by regulating its intracellular trafficking from early endosomes to the trans Golgi network versus the lysosome.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined trafficking and expression data presented in the study.

claims.claim: APP through the CRD regulates neurite growth and axon branching complexity in primary mouse cortical neurons.
claims.source: Finally, we show that APP through the CRD regulates neurite growth and axon branching complexity in primary mouse cortical neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined neurite outgrowth data showing CRD-dependent effects.

claims.claim: APP shares similarity with type I transmembrane receptors.
claims.source: The first strong evidence came from the structure of APP which shares similarity with type I transmembrane receptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about APP structure.

claims.claim: The growth factor like domain (GFLD) in the E1 region of APP could act as a ligand-binding site.
claims.source: For example the growth factor like domain (GFLD) in the E1 region of APP could act as a ligand-binding site, and disulfide bridges within the same E1 area could further facilitate ligand-induced signal transduction by stabilizing the structure of APP ectodomain (Reinhard et al., 2005; Rossjohn et al., 1999; Stahl et al., 2014; Kaden et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on structural features and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Disulfide bridges within the E1 area could facilitate ligand-induced signal transduction by stabilizing the structure of APP ectodomain.
claims.source: For example the growth factor like domain (GFLD) in the E1 region of APP could act as a ligand-binding site, and disulfide bridges within the same E1 area could further facilitate ligand-induced signal transduction by stabilizing the structure of APP ectodomain (Reinhard et al., 2005; Rossjohn et al., 1999; Stahl et al., 2014; Kaden et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on structural features and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Both APP and Notch are processed by γ-secretase and release intracellular domains (AICD and NICD) to induce transcriptional activity.
claims.source: For instance, both APP and Notch are processed by γ-secretase and release the intracellular domain AICD and NICD, respectively, to induce transcriptional activity by nuclear transfer of the ICDs (Chang et al., 2006; Ables et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The CRD is required for binding between Wnt and its receptors and co-receptors like Frizzled, Ror-2, and Musk.
claims.source: Interestingly, a conserved CRD within the E1 region of APP makes APP a putative Wnt receptor as the CRD is required for the binding between Wnt and its receptor and co-receptor like Frizzled Ror-2 and Musk (Niehrs, 2012), although the crystal structure of the APP CRD is different from that of classic Wnt receptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The crystal structure of the APP CRD is different from that of classic Wnt receptors.
claims.source: Interestingly, a conserved CRD within the E1 region of APP makes APP a putative Wnt receptor as the CRD is required for the binding between Wnt and its receptor and co-receptor like Frizzled Ror-2 and Musk (Niehrs, 2012), although the crystal structure of the APP CRD is different from that of classic Wnt receptors.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about protein structures.

claims.claim: APP might act as a conserved Wnt receptor as its CRD is highly conserved across species.
claims.source: Based on these data, we speculate that APP might act as a conserved Wnt receptor as its CRD is highly conserved across species, and that the binding may not be limited to Wnt3a or Wnt5a, but also apply to all other Wnt family members.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on the conservation of the CRD and binding data.

claims.claim: APP binding to Wnts may not be limited to Wnt3a or Wnt5a, but may also apply to all other Wnt family members.
claims.source: Based on these data, we speculate that APP might act as a conserved Wnt receptor as its CRD is highly conserved across species, and that the binding may not be limited to Wnt3a or Wnt5a, but also apply to all other Wnt family members.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on the binding data with Wnt3a and Wnt5a.

claims.claim: LRP6 can directly bind to APP.
claims.source: A recent study has shown that LRP6, the co-receptor of canonical Wnt signaling, could directly bind to APP (Elliott et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: One of the LRP6 binding sites on APP (34 amino acids) is located within the APP CRD.
claims.source: Using peptide Mapping array this group further revealed several binding sites (20–70 amino acids in length) in the ectodomain of APP, and one of the sites (34 amino acids) is located within the APP CRD.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work using peptide mapping.

claims.claim: The conflicting data in the literature about APP's role in neurite outgrowth may arise from examining different types of neurons at different time points.
claims.source: We therefore suggest that the conflicting data in the literature may arise from examining different types of neurons at different time points, where the requirement of APP may differ in a context-specific manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on the authors' observations and literature review.

claims.claim: The context specificity of APP function may in part be due to the levels and types of Wnt ligands present in the environment.
claims.source: We speculate that this context specificity may in part be due to the levels and types of Wnt ligands present in the environment.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculated based on the data showing Wnt-dependent effects on APP function.

claims.claim: In addition to proteolytic processing, the regulation of APP recycling by Wnt ligands may be crucial for its function.
claims.source: Finally, our findings suggest that in addition to the well-described proteolytic processing of APP, the regulation of its recycling by Wnt ligands may be crucial for its function.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing Wnt effects on APP trafficking and stability.

claims.claim: Wnt ligands regulate APP stability post-translationally.
claims.source: It is important to note that, like proteolytic processing, Wnt ligands regulate APP stability post-translationally, as we found no effect on App mRNA levels upon Wnt treatment.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing changes in APP protein levels without changes in mRNA levels.

claims.claim: An imbalance between Wnt3a/canonical signaling pathway and the Wnt5a/PCP signaling pathway at the initial step of amyloid beta production could trigger a vicious cycle favoring the amyloidogenic processing of APP.
claims.source: With regard to the role of APP processing in Alzheimer's disease, recently published work suggests that an imbalance between Wnt3a/canonical signaling pathway and the Wnt5a/PCP signaling pathway at the initial step of amyloid beta production could trigger a vicious cycle favoring the amyloidogenic processing of APP (Sellers et al., 2018; Elliott et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The findings that Wnt3a and Wnt5a have opposite effects on amyloid beta production provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how the normal physiological function of APP directly impacts the generation of a key marker of AD.
claims.source: Our findings that Wnt3a and Wnt5a have opposite effects on amyloid beta production provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how the normal physiological function of APP directly impacts the generation of a key marker of AD, and thus potentially links the normal activity of APP to its role in neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing opposite effects of Wnt3a and Wnt5a on Aβ production.

results.result: APPL genetically interacts with the Wnt-PCP pathway component Vang in Drosophila mushroom body β-lobe development. Loss of one copy of vang in APPL mutants produces a phenotype comparable to complete vang loss (haploinsufficiency), and APPL re-expression rescues the phenotype while Vang overexpression does not, suggesting Wnt-PCP signaling requires APPL for axonal growth regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C7 provide converging genetic evidence from Drosophila showing APPL-Vang interactions. The haploinsufficiency data (C3-C4), rescue experiments (C5-C6), and quantitative phenotypic analysis (C1-C2) collectively support the conclusion that APPL functions downstream or in parallel to Vang in the Wnt-PCP pathway.

results.result: Wnt5 acts through APPL to inhibit mushroom body β-lobe growth in a Vang-independent manner. Wnt5/vang double mutants rescue the vang phenotype, and Wnt5/APPL double mutants show no additive effect, suggesting APPL may be a Wnt5 receptor that antagonizes PCP-mediated axon growth when Vang is absent.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C16 present epistasis analysis showing that Wnt5 loss rescues vang mutants (C11) but not APPL mutants (C14), with appropriate quantitative data. The genetic logic supports the model that APPL mediates Wnt5 signaling, though the receptor claim (C16) remains speculative pending biochemical confirmation.

results.result: APP family proteins contain a conserved cysteine-rich domain (CRD) that is necessary and sufficient for binding to Wnt5a. The CRD includes 12 conserved cysteine residues with distribution similar to other PCP receptors, and deletion of the CRD abolishes Wnt5a binding in co-immunoprecipitation experiments across species (human, mouse, Drosophila).
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C21, C24 provide sequence conservation data (C17-C18) and biochemical binding evidence (C19-C21, C24) demonstrating CRD-dependent Wnt5a binding. The co-IP experiments are performed in multiple systems with appropriate controls (CRD deletion constructs), providing strong support for the binding interaction.

results.result: Wnt5a treatment reduces mouse APP (mAPP) protein stability by redirecting trafficking from the trans-Golgi network to lysosomes for degradation. This occurs without affecting early endosome or recycling endosome localization, mRNA levels, or organelle marker expression, and is reversed by lysosomal inhibition with Bafilomycin-A.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C35 provide comprehensive trafficking and stability data using immunofluorescence colocalization (C25-C28), western blots (C31), qPCR (C32), and pharmacological rescue (C34). The data consistently show Wnt5a-induced lysosomal targeting and degradation without transcriptional effects, with appropriate controls for organelle markers (C30) and mRNA levels (C32).

results.result: Wnt3a binds to mAPP via the CRD and increases APP protein levels by promoting retrograde trafficking to the trans-Golgi network. Wnt3a and Wnt5a have antagonistic effects on APP homeostasis, with simultaneous treatment neutralizing each other's effects, and retromer inhibition reversing Wnt3a's effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C47, C53-C54 demonstrate CRD-dependent Wnt3a binding (C36), increased TGN localization (C39), elevated protein levels (C42), and antagonism with Wnt5a (C45-C46). The retromer inhibitor experiment (C44) provides mechanistic insight. The data are internally consistent and supported by appropriate controls including mRNA measurements (C43, C47).

results.result: Wnt3a and Wnt5a have opposing effects on β-catenin signaling and amyloid-β production in an APP-dependent manner. Wnt3a treatment increases β-catenin in APP-WT but not APP-KO neurons, decreases Aβ40/42 production, while Wnt5a increases Aβ40/42 production.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 connect APP's role in canonical Wnt signaling (C48-C49) to Alzheimer's disease-relevant Aβ production (C50-C52). The data show APP-dependent β-catenin accumulation and opposite effects on Aβ production consistent with the trafficking data. However, the mechanistic link between trafficking and Aβ production could be more directly demonstrated.

results.result: The CRD of mAPP is required for Wnt-mediated regulation of APP trafficking and expression. In APP-KO neurons transduced with wild-type APP, Wnt3a increases and Wnt5a decreases APP levels, but these effects are abolished when neurons are transduced with CRD-deleted APP.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 provide rescue experiments demonstrating CRD requirement for Wnt effects on APP. The use of lentiviral transduction in APP-KO neurons with wild-type versus CRD-deleted constructs provides appropriate controls. Both expression (C55-C56) and trafficking (C57-C59) data support the conclusion.

results.result: At DIV3, mAPP knockout neurons show increased axonal outgrowth (total length, longest axon, branch tips) and increased primary and secondary branching compared to controls, with no effect on dendritic growth. These phenotypes are rescued by full-length APP but not CRD-deleted APP, with no effect observed at DIV2.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C70 provide detailed morphometric analysis of neurite outgrowth at DIV3. Multiple parameters consistently show increased axonal growth in APP-KO neurons (C62, C65) with CRD-dependent rescue (C64, C66). The lack of dendritic effects (C63, C69) and temporal specificity (C61) are appropriately documented. Statistical significance is reported for key comparisons.

results.result: At DIV7, mAPP knockout neurons exhibit increased axon complexity (higher ACI) due to reduced primary branches and increased secondary branches, with no change in total axonal length. Dendritic analysis shows decreased total dendritic processes due to fewer main dendrites. All phenotypes require the CRD for rescue.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C79 demonstrate a shift from overall growth effects (DIV3) to complexity effects (DIV7) in APP-KO neurons. The ACI analysis (C71, C73) provides quantitative support for altered branching patterns. Both axonal (C71-C74) and dendritic (C75-C78) phenotypes show CRD-dependent rescue, supporting the conclusion that APP's role in neuronal maturation requires the CRD (C79).

results.result: The CRD of APP is required for Wnt3a and Wnt5a to regulate neurite outgrowth in cortical neurons. At DIV3, Wnt3a increases axonal parameters in a CRD-dependent manner, while Wnt5a effects are only observed when CRD is deleted. At DIV7, Wnt3a increases axon complexity and both Wnts decrease main dendrite number in a CRD-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C88 demonstrate that Wnt effects on neurite outgrowth require the APP CRD. The data show stage-specific effects (DIV3 vs DIV7) and opposite roles for Wnt3a (promoting) versus Wnt5a (inhibiting when CRD absent) on axonal growth. The experiments use APP-KO neurons rescued with wild-type or CRD-deleted APP, providing appropriate controls.

results.result: APP functions as a conserved Wnt receptor that binds both canonical and non-canonical Wnt ligands via the CRD, regulates full-length APP levels through intracellular trafficking control, and regulates neurite growth and axon branching complexity in primary mouse cortical neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 represent the main conclusions synthesizing the study's findings. These are well-supported by the combined genetic (Drosophila), biochemical (co-IP), cell biological (trafficking), and developmental (neurite outgrowth) data presented throughout. The claims appropriately summarize the major findings without overstating the conclusions.

results.result: APP shares structural features with type I transmembrane receptors including a growth factor-like domain and disulfide bridges that could facilitate ligand binding, undergoes γ-secretase processing similar to Notch, and contains a CRD required for Wnt binding despite having a different crystal structure than classic Wnt receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 provide background context from established literature (C92, C95-C97) and structural speculation (C93-C94). The claims appropriately cite prior work and acknowledge that while APP's CRD structure differs from classic Wnt receptors (C97), it still mediates Wnt binding as demonstrated in the current study.

results.result: APP may function as a conserved Wnt receptor for multiple Wnt family members beyond Wnt3a and Wnt5a, and may interact with the canonical Wnt co-receptor LRP6, which has a binding site within the APP CRD region.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 are speculative extrapolations from the Wnt3a/Wnt5a binding data, while C100-C101 cite prior work on LRP6-APP interactions. The speculation about broader Wnt binding (C98-C99) is reasonable but untested. The LRP6 interaction (C100-C101) from prior work could be relevant but requires further investigation to understand its relationship to the CRD-Wnt binding demonstrated here.

results.result: Conflicting literature on APP's role in neurite outgrowth may arise from context-dependent effects related to neuronal type, developmental timing, and local Wnt ligand levels. APP recycling regulation by Wnts may be as important as proteolytic processing for APP function, occurring post-translationally without affecting mRNA levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C105 provide reasonable interpretations of the data in context of prior literature. The speculation about context-dependence (C102-C103) is supported by the stage-specific effects observed (DIV2 vs DIV3 vs DIV7). The importance of Wnt-regulated recycling (C104) and post-translational regulation (C105) are directly supported by the trafficking and expression data showing no mRNA changes.

results.result: An imbalance between Wnt3a/canonical and Wnt5a/PCP signaling pathways may trigger a cycle favoring amyloidogenic APP processing in Alzheimer's disease. The opposite effects of Wnt3a and Wnt5a on Aβ production provide a mechanistic framework linking APP's normal physiological function to neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C107 connect the current findings to Alzheimer's disease pathology. C106 cites prior work proposing the imbalance hypothesis, while C107 interprets the current Aβ production data (C50-C52) in this context. The data showing opposite effects of Wnt3a (decreasing) and Wnt5a (increasing) on Aβ production support this framework, though the causal link to AD pathology remains to be established.
